text: 该网页报道了考古学家 Jack Davis 和 Sharon Stocker 在希腊西南部皮洛斯、靠近“涅斯托尔宫”遗址地区，于2015年重新展开发掘时发现的一座未被破坏的青铜时代战士竖井墓，即所谓的“狮鹫战士”墓。墓中随葬有逾1400件随葬品，包括珠宝、武器、盔甲以及青铜、银和金制器皿，被希腊文化部称为近65年来希腊大陆墓葬中史前财富最显著的例证之一。文中依据与考古学家访谈，介绍了这位战士可能的身份（可能是本土“迈锡尼人”，同时认同米诺斯宗教图像），其所处的关键历史时期（迈锡尼人形成信仰体系、迈锡尼文明的早期阶段），以及该墓对理解克里特米诺斯文化向南希腊扩展和迈锡尼文明形成的重要性。文章还提到，他们在发现墓葬后又进行了一季发掘，以更好界定战士死亡与下葬年代，并计划继续研究战士生活的公元前15世纪小镇；同时介绍了他们在希腊美国考古学校框架下、与希腊文化部各部门的合作方式。后文简要概述了 Jack Davis 和 Sharon Stocker 的学术背景，并指出他们正在就此次墓葬及其中的“米诺斯风格金戒指”等发现，在希腊和国外进行系列讲座，说明该墓随葬品对理解迈锡尼文明曙光时期的艺术与宗教仪式具有前所未有的意义。

该来源是一篇2016年11月2日的 Greek News Agenda 访谈文章，主题是 Jack Davis 和 Sharon Stocker 对皮洛斯“Griffin Warrior”墓葬发现的介绍。正文称，2015年两位辛辛那提大学学者在古代皮洛斯、靠近“内斯托尔宫”遗址处恢复发掘，并在希腊文化部许可、雅典美国古典研究学院主持下发现一座青铜时代战士墓，墓内有超过1400件物品，包括珠宝、武器、盔甲以及青铜、银和金器。文章称该墓是希腊近半个世纪最丰富的墓葬发现之一，并引用希腊文化部将其称为过去65年希腊大陆墓葬中史前财富的最显著展示。访谈中 Davis 和 Stocker 表示，Griffin Warrior 可能是希腊大陆人，但在某些方面认同米诺斯宗教图像；他们还称后续发掘帮助了解战士死亡和埋葬日期，并希望进一步了解其生活的公元前15世纪城镇。正文最后称 Davis 和 Stocker 领导了发掘未受扰动竖穴墓的团队，并提到墓中发现的米诺斯风格金戒指可为迈锡尼文明黎明时期的艺术和仪式提供见解。该正文未明确提到名为“Ring of Nestor”的具体金戒指。

这篇 CNN 报道介绍了美国辛辛那提大学考古队在希腊西南部皮洛斯（Pylos）附近发现两座“蜂巢形”的青铜时代王族或“王子级”墓葬的经过与意义。文章指出，这两座约3500年前、属于迈锡尼时期的墓葬位于尼斯托尔宫附近，接近2015年发现的“格里芬战士”墓及1939年卡尔·布莱根发掘的墓区。带队的杰克·戴维斯和莎朗·斯托克等人用18个月完成了初步发掘，发现了镌刻有两头公牛与谷穗的金戒指、描绘埃及女神的金质吊坠、琥珀和紫水晶等精美随葬品，显示墓主人具有极高财富与地位。戴维斯称，这枚戒指可能是克里特或米诺斯艺术中唯一已知的谷物图像，体现畜牧与农业结合的场景。墓室穹顶在古代坍塌，留下约4万块石头需要移除，这一坍塌也在一定程度上保护墓葬免遭盗掘。考古团队借助摄影测量和数字制图记录遗物位置。希腊文化和体育部在2018年购得墓地所在地块，使新一轮发掘成为可能。文章还提到，自上一个同类重要墓葬发掘已经约50年，因而这次发现被视为异常重要，辛辛那提大学团队计划至少再在该遗址工作两年。
该文报道了一枚在希腊皮洛斯内斯托尔宫附近出土的罕见黄金印玺戒指。戒指上刻有一幅精细的祭祀场景，被认为属于迈锡尼文明。文章强调该戒指制作工艺精湛，其微观雕刻可能是借助放大工具完成的。

文章报道了一支由辛辛那提大学研究人员领导的国际考古团队在希腊西南部皮洛斯、靠近内斯托尔迈锡尼宫（阿诺·英利亚诺斯）的一处发掘中，发现了一座完整且未被洗劫的青铜时代战士竖穴墓。墓葬最初被认为是一座青铜时代房屋，但发掘过程中出土了超过1,400件随葬品，包括珠宝、武器和盔甲，以及青铜、银和金器。墓中成年男性骨骼仰卧在墓底，左侧是武器、右侧是首饰与饰物。头胸部附近有一把青铜剑（象牙柄包金）和一把金柄匕首，腿脚附近还有其他武器；胸腹上有金杯，颈部有保存完好的金项链，两枚吊坠装饰常春藤叶。其右侧及头部周围有超过一千颗由红玉髓、紫水晶、碧玉、玛瑙和金制成的珠子，附近还有四枚金戒指、银杯以及青铜碗、杯、壶和盆。墓葬年代被认为约为公元前1500年。研究团队成员包括长期参与皮洛斯区域考古项目的辛辛那提大学师生。项目致力于研究被火灾毁于约公元前1200年的内斯托尔宫，这座宫殿被称为希腊本土保存最完好的青铜时代宫殿。Shari Stocker 将这座距今约3,500年的富裕迈锡尼战士竖穴墓称为过去65年来希腊本土最壮观的史前财富展示之一。

[5][6][7][8]

While the available publications do not provide a full set of metrological data, the ring is consistently presented as a substantial gold object whose dimensions exceed those of many contemporary signet rings, contributing to its prominence in the scholarly literature on Mycenaean glyptic. title: Iconography and interpretations
content:
The engraved scene on the Ring of Nestor has been the focus of extensive iconographic analysis. In the CMS publications and later studies, the composition is often described as a 
world-tree
 scene centred on a stylised tree or plant, around which stand or move a series of human, animal and hybrid figures. A. G. Vlachopoulos notes that the central arboreal motif, flanked by figures that appear to approach or interact with it, recalls Near Eastern and Aegean images associated with sacred trees or pillars, though he emphasises that the precise narrative content of the scene remains uncertain. Another study devoted to the iconography of the ring highlights the presence of a guardian figure and a motif interpreted by some as a scorpion, positioned strategically within the composition and possibly serving an apotropaic or protective function. [5][6][7][8]

The human or humanlike figures on the ring have been variously described as deities, officiants or elite individuals engaged in a ritual performance. Some scholars see in the arrangement of the figures and the central tree an evocation of a ritual approach to a sacred object or space, with gestures that may indicate offering, adoration or dance. Others prefer to treat the scene as a more general expression of the relationship between humans, animals and a conceptualised natural or cosmic order, given the absence of accompanying inscriptions or unequivocal mythological markers. [5][6][7][8]

Interpretations of the supposed scorpion motif also differ. In some analyses, the form is identified as a scorpion-like creature that acts as a guardian or boundary marker near the world-tree, possibly reflecting broader eastern Mediterranean traditions in which scorpions and other dangerous animals are associated with liminal zones and protection of sacred spaces. Other scholars are more cautious, suggesting that the shape may be a highly stylised animal or abstract sign whose identification as a scorpion is not secure. In all cases, authors underline that the reading of individual details must be considered within the holistic composition and the conventions of Creto-Mycenaean glyptic. [5][6][7][8]

No inscription is reported on the ring in the CMS catalogues or in the detailed iconographic and authenticity studies, and interpretations therefore rely entirely on visual analysis and comparison with other Aegean and Near Eastern images. This lack of textual guidance encourages a range of hypotheses about the meaning and function of the scene but also limits the degree of certainty with which specific religious or mythological narratives can be proposed. [5][6][7][8]

content:
The published scholarship on the Ring of Nestor provides only limited information about the circumstances of its discovery and early history. Ingo Pinis article on the ring, as well as subsequent discussions of CMS I, 179, treat the piece in connection with the so-called Tiryns treasure, linking it to material said to have been found at or near the site of Tiryns in the early twentieth century. References to a 1915 discovery by Apostolos Arvanitopoulos appear in this context, but the available evidence does not include a detailed primary excavation report that would securely document the tomb, hoard or assemblage in which the ring was found. [5][6][8][10][12][13][14][15][16][17][18]

Because of these gaps, authors who analyse the Ring of Nestor emphasise that its archaeological context is not firmly established. The ring is sometimes associated in secondary literature with broader discussions of early Mycenaean elite burials and treasures from sites such as Tiryns and Pylos, but these associations rely on comparisons of style and iconography rather than on explicit statements that the ring formed part of a particular grave or hoard. The Pylos Regional Archaeological Project and related publications on the so-called Griffin Warrior tomb and nearby tholos burials at Ano Englianos have drawn attention to richly furnished shaft graves containing multiple gold signet rings, yet the sources documenting those excavations do not identify any of the rings as the 
Ring of Nestor
 or as CMS I, 179. [5][6][8][10][12][13][14][15][16][17][18]

As a result, modern discussions often distinguish between the secure archaeological contexts of well-documented excavations and the more fragile reconstructions of provenance for pieces like the Ring of Nestor, whose early history depends on later cataloguing and museum records. Some scholars note that uncertainty about the discovery context has implications for how the ring is used in broader historical arguments about regional workshops, patterns of elite exchange or the development of Mycenaean religious imagery, and they advocate a cautious approach that acknowledges these limitations. title: Scholarly debate on authenticity and dating
content:
The Ring of Nestor has been at the centre of a sustained scholarly debate about its authenticity, chronology and place within Creto-Mycenaean glyptic. In his article in the Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Ingo Pini raised questions about the rings authenticity, scrutinising aspects of the engraving technique, stylistic features and reported provenance. Pini compared the rings iconography and execution with securely provenanced Mycenaean signet rings and suggested that certain elements might indicate modern intervention or even fabrication, particularly when considered against the incomplete documentation of the rings discovery. These concerns led some researchers to treat the Ring of Nestor with caution in discussions of Mycenaean iconography and to call for further technical analysis. [5][6][7][8]

More recent work by A. G. Vlachopoulos revisits the question of authenticity and argues for a more nuanced view. Vlachopoulos analyses the ring within the broader corpus of early Mycenaean and Creto-Mycenaean glyptic, drawing attention to parallels in composition, motif selection and engraving style that, in his assessment, support the rings placement in the 16th–15th century BC. While acknowledging the problems posed by the incomplete provenance record, he contends that the combination of stylistic and iconographic features is consistent with other early Mycenaean gold rings and that accusations of forgery or extensive modern reworking are not substantiated by the available evidence. [5][6][7][8]

Additional studies focusing on the iconography of the ring have tended to align with the view that the piece belongs, at least in its present form, to the early Late Bronze Age Aegean glyptic tradition, though some authors maintain reservations about the possibility of later modifications or restorations. Discussions of the ring in the context of CMS I, 179 and related catalogues generally retain its attribution as a Mycenaean gold signet ring while noting the disputed aspects of its history. [5][6][7][8]

The debate over authenticity intersects with broader methodological issues in Aegean archaeology, including the evaluation of unprovenanced or poorly documented artifacts and the criteria used to distinguish genuine Bronze Age objects from modern creations. Scholars working on the Ring of Nestor often frame their conclusions with explicit caveats, emphasising that assessments of authenticity and dating are probabilistic and remain open to revision in light of future analytical or archival discoveries. [5][6][7][8]

title: Cultural significance and reception
content:
The Ring of Nestor occupies an important place in the study of Aegean iconography because its complex scene brings together several themes that recur in Minoan and Mycenaean art: sacred vegetation, processional or ritual gestures, guardian animals and the display of elite status through gold signet rings. Researchers have used the ring as a case study for examining how Mycenaean elites adopted, adapted or reinterpreted visual traditions associated with Minoan Crete during the early Late Bronze Age. Its imagery is also relevant to discussions of cross-cultural contacts in the eastern Mediterranean, since the world-tree and guardian motifs invite comparison with Near Eastern compositions while remaining embedded in Aegean glyptic conventions. [5][6][7][8]

The ring’s scholarly significance is inseparable from its debated status. Because the discovery context and authenticity have both been questioned, the artifact is frequently cited not only for its imagery but also as an example of the evidentiary challenges involved in interpreting poorly provenanced objects. In this respect, the Ring of Nestor has become part of a wider conversation about the standards of proof required for using individual artifacts in reconstructions of Bronze Age religion, social hierarchy and artistic exchange. [5][6][7][8]

The ring is less securely documented in public-facing institutional records than some other Aegean gold signet rings, and the available sources do not provide a firmly supported statement of its current museum location or continuous provenance. For this reason, summaries of the artifact should avoid presenting its ownership history, findspot or archaeological assemblage as settled unless supported by a specific catalogue or archival source. Its cultural significance therefore lies both in the interpretive possibilities opened by its elaborate imagery and in the caution it demands from scholars handling objects with incomplete documentation. [5][6][7][8]

One detailed study of CMS I, 179 notes that the ring was unearthed in December 1915 by Apostolos Arvanitopoulos and records dimensions of 3.5 by 5.7 cm, an annulus diameter of 2.2 cm and a weight of 82.95 g, but does not provide a full excavation report for the tomb or hoard in which it was found. [5][6][8][10][12][13][14][15][16][17][18]

Because of these gaps, authors who analyse the Ring of Nestor emphasise that its archaeological context is not firmly established. The ring is sometimes associated in secondary literature with broader discussions of early Mycenaean elite burials and treasures from sites such as Tiryns and Pylos, but these associations rely on comparisons of style and iconography rather than on explicit statements that the ring formed part of a particular grave or hoard. The Pylos Regional Archaeological Project and related work around the Palace of Nestor at Ano Englianos have documented numerous prehistoric and historical sites in Messenia, including an intensive survey of an area surrounding the palace and investigations along the ridge of Ano Englianos, but these publications do not connect the Ring of Nestor to any specific locality within that landscape. [5][6][8][10][12][13][14][15][16][17][18]

Separate excavations conducted since 2015 at Pylos by Jack L. Davis and Sharon Stocker uncovered the shaft grave of the so-called Griffin Warrior and nearby tholos tombs, which contained more than 1,400 grave goods including jewels, weapons, armour and metal vessels, along with several gold signet rings. These finds have been widely discussed as evidence for early Mycenaean elite burial practices and for interactions between Minoan and Mycenaean cultural traditions, but the reports and popular accounts describing the Griffin Warrior assemblage do not identify any of the rings as CMS VI, no. 277 or as the "Ring of Nestor". [5][6][8][10][12][13][14][15][16][17][18]

Modern discussions therefore often distinguish between the secure archaeological contexts of well-documented excavations such as the Griffin Warrior tomb and the more tentative reconstructions of provenance for pieces like the Ring of Nestor, whose early history depends largely on later cataloguing and museum records. Scholars note that uncertainty about the discovery context has implications for how the ring is used in broader historical arguments about regional workshops, patterns of elite exchange or the development of Mycenaean religious imagery, and they advocate a cautious approach that acknowledges these limitations. [5][6][8][10][12][13][14][15][16][17][18]

title: Scholarly debate on authenticity and dating
content:
The Ring of Nestor has been at the centre of a sustained scholarly debate about its authenticity, chronology and place within Creto-Mycenaean glyptic. In his article in the Oxford Journal of Archaeology, Ingo Pini raised questions about the ring’s authenticity, scrutinising aspects of the engraving technique, stylistic features and reported provenance. Pini compared the ring’s iconography and execution with securely provenanced Mycenaean signet rings and suggested that certain elements might indicate modern intervention or even fabrication, particularly when considered against the incomplete documentation of the ring’s discovery. These concerns led some researchers to treat the Ring of Nestor with caution in discussions of Mycenaean iconography and to call for further technical analysis. [5][6][7][8]

More recent work by A. G. Vlachopoulos revisits the question of authenticity and argues for a different assessment. Vlachopoulos analyses the ring within the broader corpus of early Mycenaean and Creto-Mycenaean glyptic, drawing attention to parallels in composition, motif selection and engraving style that, in his assessment, support the ring’s placement in the 16th–15th century BC. He emphasises that the ring, measuring 3.29 by 2.18 cm, belongs among the largest Aegean signet rings and that its iconography, including the guardian figure and scorpion motif, fits into a network of Bronze Age Aegean images rather than suggesting a modern pastiche. While acknowledging the problems posed by the incomplete provenance record, Vlachopoulos contends that accusations of forgery or extensive modern reworking are not substantiated by the available evidence and reports that his research supports the ring’s authenticity. [5][6][7][8]

Additional studies focusing on the iconography of the ring have tended to align with the view that the piece belongs, at least in its present form, to the early Late Bronze Age Aegean glyptic tradition, though some authors continue to discuss the possibility of later modifications or restorations. Discussions of the ring in the context of CMS I, 179 and related catalogues generally retain its attribution as a Mycenaean gold signet ring while noting the disputed aspects of its history. [5][6][7][8]

The debate over authenticity intersects with broader methodological issues in Aegean archaeology, including the evaluation of unprovenanced or poorly documented artifacts and the criteria used to distinguish genuine Bronze Age objects from modern creations. Scholars working on the Ring of Nestor often frame their conclusions with explicit caveats, emphasising that assessments of authenticity and dating are based on current evidence and remain open to revision in light of future analytical or archival discoveries. [5][6][7][8]

title: Cultural significance and reception
content:
The Ring of Nestor occupies a notable place in the study of Aegean iconography because its complex scene brings together several themes that recur in Minoan and Mycenaean art: sacred vegetation, processional or ritual gestures, guardian animals and the display of elite status through gold signet rings. Researchers have used the ring as a case study for examining how Mycenaean elites adopted, adapted or reinterpreted visual traditions associated with Minoan Crete during the early Late Bronze Age. Its imagery is also relevant to discussions of cross-cultural contacts in the eastern Mediterranean, since the world-tree and guardian motifs invite comparison with Near Eastern compositions while remaining embedded in Aegean glyptic conventions. [5][6][7][8]

The ring’s scholarly significance is inseparable from its debated status. Because the discovery context and authenticity have both been questioned at various points in the literature, the artifact is frequently cited not only for its imagery but also as an example of the evidentiary challenges involved in interpreting poorly documented objects. In this respect, the Ring of Nestor has become part of a wider conversation about the standards of proof required for using individual artifacts in reconstructions of Bronze Age religion, social hierarchy and artistic exchange. [5][6][7][8]

The ring is less securely documented in public-facing institutional records than some other Aegean gold signet rings, and the available sources do not provide a firmly supported statement of its current museum location or continuous provenance. For this reason, summaries of the artifact in modern scholarship typically avoid presenting its ownership history, findspot or archaeological assemblage as settled unless supported by a specific catalogue or archival source. Its cultural significance therefore lies both in the interpretive possibilities opened by its elaborate imagery and in the caution it demands from scholars handling objects with incomplete documentation. [5][6][7][8]

text: 本论文集《Art of the Hellenistic Kingdoms: From Pergamon to Rome》基于在大都会艺术博物馆举办、与展览“Pergamon and the Hellenistic Kingdoms of the Ancient World”配套的为期两天的学术研讨会所发表的论文编纂而成。

qualifiers: 时间段：323 B.C. 至 30 B.C.
主题范围：希腊化艺术与文化
text: 该卷包含二十篇学术论文，讨论的时间范围为自公元前323年亚历山大大帝去世至公元前30年克利奥帕特拉自杀之间约三百年的希腊化时期艺术与文化。

qualifiers: 展览地点：The Metropolitan Museum of Art, New York
展览时间：2016年
范围限定：美国境内的大型国际借展展览
text: 展览“Pergamon and the Hellenistic Kingdoms of the Ancient World”是美国首次以希腊化艺术为主题的大型国际借展展览。

qualifiers: 展览主题：佩加蒙与希腊化诸王国艺术
借展机构地域：希腊、意大利、其他欧洲国家、摩洛哥、突尼斯、美国
text: 该展览特别强调阿塔罗斯王朝首都佩加蒙，展示了通过希腊、意大利、其他欧洲国家、摩洛哥、突尼斯和美国等多家重要博物馆借展而来的多样化希腊化艺术品。

qualifiers: 时间定义：323 B.C.–30 B.C.
评价：关键时期但较少受到传统研究关注
text: 希腊化时期被界定为亚历山大大帝于公元前323年去世到托勒密王朝女王克利奥帕特拉于公元前30年自杀之间的大约三个世纪，是希腊艺术史上一个关键但传统上关注较少的时期。

qualifiers: 亚历山大在位时间：356–323 B.C.
地理范围：从希腊和小亚细亚，经埃及和近东，至印度河流域
text: 亚历山大大帝的征服将希腊文明向东传播至前波斯帝国的领土，开辟了新的贸易路线并促进了跨文化交流，对古代世界产生了深远影响。

qualifiers: 形成时间：亚历山大死后，尤其是公元前三世纪上半叶
地理与政权：Seleucids, Ptolemies, Antigonids, Attalid kingdom of Pergamon
text: 在亚历山大去世后，其将领“继业者”将其庞大帝国分割成多个新王国，其中形成的主要王朝包括近东的塞琉古王朝、埃及的托勒密王朝和马其顿的安提柯王朝，而佩加蒙的阿塔罗斯王朝等较小王国在公元前三世纪上半叶从塞琉古王国中分离出来。

qualifiers: 时间：希腊化时期
赞助主体：希腊化王室
典型机构：亚历山大和佩加蒙的图书馆
text: 希腊化诸王国财富与权力的集中促进了艺术的空前发展，王室赞助下形成了最早的大型图书馆、艺术收藏与“博物馆”等文化机构。

qualifiers: 媒介：青铜、釉陶、玻璃、大理石、银器、陶土等
立足材料：Metropolitan Museum 的馆藏
text: 本卷多篇文章通过大都会艺术博物馆丰富的希腊化艺术藏品，探讨王权自我呈现、钱币、宝石、马赛克、雕塑、器皿与壁画等媒介中图像学与风格的关键元素及其技术创新。

qualifiers: 展览地点：The Metropolitan Museum of Art
展厅内容：Age of Alexander
text: 展览“Pergamon and the Hellenistic Kingdoms of the Ancient World”在首个展厅中以亚历山大大帝时代的作品开篇，将他作为后继者们效仿并与之建立联系的首要典范。

qualifiers: 币种：Manbog coinage, Elephant coinage
时间：可能为亚历山大在世期间
文化特征：希腊与波斯传统融合
text: 乌特·瓦滕贝格在本卷第一篇论文中研究了两类被称为“Manbog”币和“大象”币的稀有币制，这些钱币很可能铸造于亚历山大在世期间，并体现了古典希腊与波斯文化传统的融合。
limitations: 铸造时间被描述为“probably minted”，具有推测性

qualifiers: 诗人：Poseidippos of Pella (ca. 310–240 B.C.)
纸草收藏机构：University of Milan
服务对象：Ptolemaic kings in Alexandria
text: 杰弗里·斯皮尔的论文利用米兰大学新近购得的一份纸草文书，研究马其顿诗人波塞底波斯为托勒密王室创作的铭诗，这些诗歌频繁提及贵重宝石及其在宫廷中的使用，显示宝石与诗歌共同用于颂扬赞助人并体现王权与权威。

qualifiers: 媒介：mosaics, sculptures, luxury arts
主题：视觉与文字的互动，爱情主题
text: 克里斯汀·孔多莱翁在论文中探讨了希腊化时期诗歌与艺术中的“视觉谜语”和文字游戏，利用马赛克、雕塑和奢侈品的图像与诗歌文本配对，尤其关注“爱”这一在后期罗马对希腊化艺术和诗歌的再现中同样重要的主题。

qualifiers: 发掘机构：German Archaeological Institute
时间跨度：近140年
对象：佩加蒙城考古遗迹
text: 佩加蒙因其首都城市长期、系统的考古发掘而被视为研究希腊化王国最重要的案例之一，大部分发掘由德国考古研究所近一百四十年来主导。

qualifiers: 地点：Pergamon Museum, Berlin
内容：Gigantomachy frieze, Telephos frieze, roof sculpture
text: 佩加蒙博物馆中的佩加蒙大祭坛被描述为希腊化时期最令人印象深刻的建筑纪念物之一，其巨型浮雕描绘诸神与巨人的战斗，并在柏林得到强有力的重建展示。

qualifiers: 限制：Gigantomachy slabs built into museum walls, could not travel
补充展品：Telephos frieze slabs, rooftop sculpture fragments
text: 由于佩加蒙博物馆正在进行大规模翻新，内嵌于馆墙的巨人战浮雕板石无法外借，但展览通过借展部分碎片、Telephos 浮雕和屋顶三维雕塑，以及创新的展陈设计，仍向纽约观众传达了大祭坛的宏伟与力量感。

text: 导论指出，希腊化世界疆域从西端的赫拉克勒斯之柱（直布罗陀海峡）跨越地中海，经过小亚细亚和近东直到印度河流域，构成一个王国众多、同盟关系多变且复杂度极高的历史背景。

title: Uncovering the Early Mycenaeans – Popular Archeology

text: 该文为期刊论文《The Pylos Regional Archaeological Project: Part I》中一段内容，介绍了PRAP（Pylos Regional Archaeological Project）在西弥塞尼亚、以涅斯托尔宫（Palace of Nestor）为中心区域开展系统地表调查的背景、目标、方法与与前人工作的关系。文章说明项目自1990年正式组织，在1991年一次“reconnaissance”试探性季以及1992–1994三季主要田野工作期间，强化调查约40平方公里，重点覆盖现代Hora镇周边及整个Englianos山脊，并在额外约30平方公里对既知遗址做补充调查与精确界定。文中回顾了战前及UMME（University of Minnesota Messenia Expedition）等前期考古工作的贡献与局限，认为UMME为迈锡尼时期地理与聚落格局研究奠定基础，但因其调查偏广泛、不够密集，且有明显的青铜时代偏向，后期时期资料不均衡。PRAP旨在以更密集、多策略的地表调查与自然环境研究（地质、地貌、地球物理、古植物学）弥补这些缺口，覆盖史前至历史各时期的人类占用与土地利用，强调区域性与历时性视角。文本还细述了1991年侦察季的具体目标（界定调查区、复查既知遗址、评估Englianos山脊表面遗存并规划勘探与地球物理工作）、正式调查区划定及原计划与实际完成面积的差异，并将PRAP定位为在UMME基础上的“第二阶段”研究，用于检验前人方法的局限、修正区域聚落与人口重构。

该 Instagram 帖子由波兰考古研究所雅典分部账号发布，介绍在雅典国家考古博物馆举行的临时展览“Pylos of Nestor: A Mycenaean Kingdom Revealed”。展览展示来自梅塞尼亚的 200 多件独特文物，包括一枚来自皮洛斯英格利亚诺斯山未被盗掘墓葬的玛瑙印章，被认为是史前爱琴海艺术的杰作。展览强调考古研究过程本身，通过展示发掘日记片段、绘图和档案照片，让观众了解从发现、记录到解释的完整发掘流程，并将文物与发现它们的考古人员关联起来。展览叙事被描述为一次穿越时间与空间的旅程，从分散的权力中心到阿诺英格利亚诺斯宫殿的出现，该宫殿与荷马史诗中的涅斯托尔王国传统相关。展览地点在雅典国家考古博物馆，持续时间为 2026 年 5 月 26 日至 2026 年 9 月 31 日，相关网站为 namuseum.gr。

Paul Getty Museum 与希腊文化部共同组织的展览“The Kingdom of Pylos: Warrior-Princes of Mycenaean Greece”，展览展示了梅塞尼亚地区晚青铜时代的文物，强调内斯托尔宫殿和“Griffin Warrior”墓的重要性，以及随葬品所反映的当时文化与经济交流。页面没有提供完整文章正文，只有这一段 AI 增强的标题和描述，以及 Scribd 平台的通用界面与菜单信息。

该文介绍了位于希腊伯罗奔尼撒地区皮洛斯（Pylos）附近、与“涅斯托尔宫殿”相关的一系列迈锡尼早期考古发现，包括两座新近发掘的蜂巢形（tholos）家族墓葬（Tholos VI 和 Tholos VII）以及2015年发现的“狮鹫战士”（Griffin Warrior）竖井墓。文中描述了发掘团队（辛辛那提大学的 Jack Davis 和 Sharon Stocker 及学生志愿者）如何在覆盖葡萄藤的地块下清除成千上万块塌落石块，揭示深至约15英尺的墓室结构，出土大量金箔碎片、珠饰、法昂斯、青铜与银器，以及带有狮身神兽（genii）、公牛和疑似埃及女神哈索尔图像的宝石图章、金戒指和吊坠等高等级随葬品，反映出葬者家族的显赫地位和广泛的东地中海贸易网络（如波罗的海琥珀、埃及紫水晶和进口红玉髓）。文中还回顾了 1939 年 Carl Blegen 发掘“涅斯托尔宫殿”和 Tholos IV 的历史，指出出土约1000块线形文字 B 泥板，表明该宫殿是迈锡尼时期麦西尼亚地区的行政、政治和财政中心。关于“狮鹫战士”墓，文中详列一具约30–35岁、身高约5.5英尺的成年男性骨骼及其随葬物清单，包括三英尺长的长剑、匕首、多件青铜武器、四枚实心金指环、金项链、金银杯、数十枚米诺斯风格图章石、象牙雕件与梳子、上千颗各类宝石珠、青铜薄带以及野猪獠牙等，并描述通过保存状况和空间关系推断随葬品原始摆放方式和葬者面容特征。文末从这些墓葬的规模、财富与被反复扰动、掠夺的情况推断：晚青铜时代早期，皮洛斯区域存在多支争夺权势的精英家族，“狮鹫战士”可能代表其中最终脱颖而出的高权力人物，显示皮洛斯在迈锡尼文明成型阶段已是重要权力中心，且当地精英接收来自整个东地中海及更远地区的奢侈品。

qualifiers: 项目地点：西弥塞尼亚，以涅斯托尔宫为中心区域
研究方法：主要为地表调查
text: Pylos Regional Archaeological Project（PRAP）在1990年秋正式组织，其目的主要是通过地表调查研究以涅斯托尔宫为中心的西弥塞尼亚地区的史前与历史聚落和土地利用史。

qualifiers: 时间范围：1991–1994年夏季
调查类型：intensive surface survey
面积：约40 km²
text: 在1991年一次“reconnaissance”试探性调查和1992–1994三季主要田野工作期间，PRAP对约40平方公里区域进行了强化地表调查，包括现代Hora镇以北、东、南和西的区域以及Englianos山脊的上下段。

qualifiers: 范围：在intensively surveyed的约40 km²内
对象：已知考古遗址数量
text: PRAP的田野工作使该项目强化调查区域内已知遗址数量约增加了一倍。

qualifiers: 面积：约30 km²
工作内容：复查已知遗址，界定空间范围与年代构成
text: 除强化调查外，PRAP还在额外约30平方公里区域对几乎所有已知遗址进行了复查，以更精确界定其空间范围与年代组成。

qualifiers: 自然科学方向：geological, geomorphological, geophysical, paleobotanical
开始时间：1991年起
text: 自1991年起，PRAP支持地质、地貌、地球物理和古植物学等自然环境研究，这些工作由Eberhard Zangger组织和协调。

qualifiers: 时间对比：战前与20世纪后期
区域对比：弥塞尼亚与Corinthia、Argolid
text: 在第二次世界大战之前，弥塞尼亚地区的考古工作基本处于边缘地位，但到20世纪后期，该地区在晚期史前时期的研究信息量仅次于东北伯罗奔尼撒。

text: 美国明尼苏达大学弥塞尼亚考察（UMME）在20世纪60年代发起，系统调查了晚期青铜时代由涅斯托尔宫控制的区域，并强调区域而非单遗址、历时而非共时的研究视角。

qualifiers: 方法特征：extensive survey

qualifiers: 三条研究路线：intensive regional survey, palace-adjacent investigations, inventory survey of known sites
text: PRAP提出三条主要研究路线：围绕涅斯托尔宫的大范围强化调查以涵盖早期迈锡尼中心、一个希腊–罗马城市及其腹地与至少一个中世纪村落；对宫殿直接周边进行地表采集、地球物理与地貌研究；以及对Pylos地区既知史前和历史遗址进行清单式复查与采集。

qualifiers: 时间跨度：prehistoric to historical
理论背景：Annales school, longue durée
text: PRAP规划时即决定覆盖西弥塞尼亚从史前到历史各时期的人类占用，以响应Annales学派关于长期人与环境关系的研究取向。
